A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Analog Foundation Models, retaining the same core method, models and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model evaluations, hardware-noise simulations, training ablations, RoBERTa/GLUE experiments and MATH-500 test-time scaling results.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds device-noise, drift, tiling, quantization and convergence studies, plus original throughput and energy-efficiency simulations.

M1.justification: The proposed synthetic-data distillation pipeline, input-range learning, output quantization, Gaussian noise injection and iterative weight clipping remain unchanged in Section 3.1 and Equations 1–4. The additional precision and hardware-mapping experiments test configurations of the retained approach.

E1.justification: The language benchmarks and training corpora are retained, but deployment coverage expands substantially. Appendices F.1–F.2 add ReRAM noise, stronger PCM noise, and combined programming noise, read noise and conductance drift from one minute to one year after programming.

E2.justification: The predictive comparisons retain off-the-shelf models, LLM-QAT and SpinQuant. Appendix K adds a quantitative energy-efficiency comparison against a hypothetical INT8 GPU operating at 100% utilization. This is an additional estimated hardware comparator, not a measured GPU experiment.

E3.justification: New protocols include 1.5×/2× PCM noise, drift time points, 512×512 tile mapping, 7-bit input training on 1B tokens, and simulation with 256 prefill tokens, 64 generated tokens and batch size four. Section 3.2 also removes v1's explicit noiseless-zero-weight exception, changing the documented evaluation assumption without establishing which experiments were rerun. Existing benchmark prompts and core training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: The original Appendix A–C studies remain. New Appendices D, F, G and H investigate clipping's relationship to SNR and quantization error, robustness across device and temporal noise conditions, input precision, tiled deployment and training convergence. These substantially extend the mechanistic and sensitivity analyses.

E5.justification: The existing ten-seed noise evaluations and five-repeat test-time scaling protocol are retained. Table 15 newly attaches uncertainty to previously reported aggregate PCM averages: Analog FM is 66.33 ± 0.86, whereas v1 Table 1 gives the aggregate as 66.33 without uncertainty. The aggregation procedure is not explained, and no increase in repetitions is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises numerous entries: Phi-3's noisy average changes from 62.92 to 62.02, and its Analog FM counterpart from 66.33 to 66.22. New Tables 15–19 add substantial results, including ReRAM averages of 65.57 for Analog FM versus 58.52 for LLM-QAT. Appendix K reports simulated throughput of 2554.43 tokens/s and efficiency of 199.78 tokens/s/W. These are revised or additional outcomes, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The training equations, additive/affine noise definitions and fitted PCM-noise polynomial are retained. The new SNR and quantization material provides empirical measurements and mechanism explanations, without adding formal theoretical results, proofs or derivations.

C1.justification: The introduction changes the test-time scaling contribution from models that 'scale better' to models that 'benefit equally,' while retaining the stated 4.74% advantage. This locally qualifies the claim, although the abstract and conclusion retain stronger scaling language. The other main contributions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations connecting clipping, conductance-dependent SNR and tiling, and explains why hardware calibration complements HWA training. It interprets generalization across memory technologies and temporal noise. Limitations now explicitly include approximately threefold linear-kernel overhead, slower convergence, and the simulated rather than physical nature of the efficiency evidence.

D1.justification: The original training hyperparameters, resource descriptions, prompts and code link are retained. v3 adds implementation references for comprehensive noise modeling and architectural simulation, clarifies static versus temporal noise, and discloses kernel overhead and the Python simulator's sequence-length limitation.

R1.justification: v3 adds references on programming/read noise, temperature effects, IR-drop, conductance drift and the IBM analog hardware acceleration kit, expanding the hardware background and calibration discussion. Its central positioning relative to LLM-QAT, SpinQuant and Zhang et al. remains intact.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section structure are retained. Selected background, results and limitations paragraphs are expanded; noise-model documentation moves within Appendix E; training and scaling details move to Appendices I and J. The conference footer and acknowledgments are also updated.

P2.justification: v3 adds three multi-panel figures for SNR, quantization error and convergence, plus five tables for additional hardware experiments. All eight original figures are retained; the pipeline and noise-model figures are relocated and renumbered. The unchanged detailed MATH-500 table moves from Table 15 to Table 20.

improvement.justification: The new device, drift and tiling studies address v1's limited validation of deployment conditions, while the mechanism analyses and training-cost disclosures improve understanding. However, v3 leaves unexplained differences between Table 1 and appendix PCM baselines. Section 4.1 also claims a maximum 12.87-point Phi-3 advantage over LLM-QAT, whereas Table 1 supports 11.25 points. The expanded validation provides a net benefit, moderated by these reporting inconsistencies.
